boards.title: 10 Blocks Off Campus, One Reason Each
boards.description: Ten named stops along Annville corridors beside Lebanon Valley College, each drawn from the Annville Heritage Trail.

cards.title: The Allen Theatre: Annville’s revival marker
cards.subtitle: East Main Street corridor — 36 E. Main St.
cards.notes: Walk the East Main Street block to see the theatre identified by the heritage trail as part of Annville’s 1995 reopening story.
cards.short_summary: A historic cinema building on the East Main Street corridor.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail identifies The Allen Theatre at 36 E. Main St. and dates its reopening as the Allen to September 21, 1995.
cards.access_notes: Check the theatre’s current program before planning an interior visit.

cards.title: Annville United Methodist Church: blue-marble façade
cards.subtitle: North College Avenue corridor — 1 N. College Ave.
cards.notes: Pause at the College Avenue corner and look for the church’s Pennsylvania blue-marble construction noted on the heritage trail.
cards.short_summary: A 1912 church at the College Avenue and Main Street corner.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail lists Annville United Methodist Church at 1 N. College Ave., dedicated in 1912 and built with King of Prussia marble.
cards.access_notes: Observe the exterior from public areas; verify service or visitor access separately.

cards.title: Kettering Corner: a circa-1780 storefront conversion
cards.subtitle: West Main Street corridor — 104 W. Main St.
cards.notes: Follow West Main Street to this named corner and compare its Georgian details with the trail’s account of its first-floor store use.
cards.short_summary: A named historic corner building on West Main Street.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail identifies Kettering Corner at 104 W. Main St., describing Georgian decoration and a first floor later converted to a store.
cards.access_notes: Exterior viewing is the appropriate default; individual occupants control any interior access.

cards.title: Batdorf Building: stonework from 1810
cards.subtitle: West Main Street corridor — 103 W. Main St.
cards.notes: On the West Main Street block, look closely at the building’s cut-stone front and the contrasting rubble-stone side walls.
cards.short_summary: A stone commercial-era building with documented construction details.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail places the Batdorf Building at 103 W. Main St., dates it to 1810, and distinguishes its cut-stone front from rubble side walls.
cards.access_notes: View architectural details from public sidewalks; check the current occupant for entry information.

cards.title: Heilman House: Victorian addition on an earlier house
cards.subtitle: West Main Street corridor — 115 W. Main St.
cards.notes: Keep west along Main Street and look for the ornate Victorian addition that the trail says joined an early stone house.
cards.short_summary: A layered historic house with both early-stone and Victorian-era elements.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail identifies Heilman House at 115 W. Main St.; it says the Victorian addition was built in 1901 and the original stone house dates as early as 1810.
cards.access_notes: Exterior viewing only unless the current property occupant offers access.

cards.title: Oddfellows’ Hall: former jail and auditorium
cards.subtitle: West Main Street corridor — 219 W. Main St.
cards.notes: Continue along West Main Street and use the trail’s history to spot a building once shared by civic, fire, and lodge uses.
cards.short_summary: A former multi-use civic hall on West Main Street.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail lists Oddfellows’ Hall at 219 W. Main St.; it says the first floor held the town jail and Rescue Fire Company and the second floor was a public auditorium.
cards.access_notes: The trail notes that the building now contains living units; view it from public areas.

cards.title: Washington House: an 18th-century hotel form
cards.subtitle: West Main Street corridor — 245 W. Main St.
cards.notes: At this West Main Street address, look for the original corner doorway, pent eaves, and large stone lintels described by the trail.
cards.short_summary: A historic hotel building with surviving exterior features.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail identifies Washington House at 245 W. Main St. as an attractive hotel built around 1795 and notes its original corner entrance and stone lintels.
cards.access_notes: View exterior features from the public sidewalk; verify any current business access independently.

cards.title: Log House: pre-Revolution saltbox profile
cards.subtitle: West Main Street corridor — 437 W. Main St.
cards.notes: Extend west on Main Street to identify the steep saltbox roof and split-wood red-oak shingles described on the heritage trail.
cards.short_summary: A named pre-Revolution-style house on the West Main Street corridor.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail lists the Log House at 437 W. Main St. as a pre-Revolution New England saltbox-style house with a steep roof and split-wood red-oak shingles.
cards.access_notes: Exterior viewing only; this is a residential property.

cards.title: Flour Mill: Annville’s long-running milling site
cards.subtitle: West Queen Street corridor — 545 W. Queen St.
cards.notes: Detour one block south of West Main Street to see the four-story frame-and-stone mill complex noted by the heritage trail.
cards.short_summary: A historic mill complex on the West Queen Street corridor.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail identifies the Flour Mill at 545 W. Queen St. and states that a precursor is attested as early as March 10, 1752.
cards.access_notes: View the complex from public areas; confirm any on-site access with its current operator.

cards.title: Jerusalem Cemetery: an early Annville burial ground
cards.subtitle: South White Oak Street corridor — 200 S. White Oak St.
cards.notes: Take South White Oak Street to this named cemetery site and read the trail’s account of Annville pioneers buried there in the 1800s.
cards.short_summary: A documented early burial-ground site on South White Oak Street.
cards.evidence_claim: The heritage trail lists Jerusalem Cemetery at 200 S. White Oak St. and says many Annville pioneers were buried there between 1804 and 1895.
cards.access_notes: Treat the site as a cemetery and follow posted rules and any access restrictions.
